conversation.content:
Good morning—my name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through a short screening today called the **Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale**, or EPDS. It’s simply a 10-question check-in about how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived, so we can make sure you’re getting the support you deserve. Everything you share stays between you, me, and the clinical team, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll go one question at a time, and we can pause whenever you need.

Let’s start gently:  

Over the past seven days, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult lately?

Honestly? I’ve laughed a couple of times—like when my husband made that silly face trying to get the baby to burp—but most of the day it feels like I’m too tired or pre-occupied to find much funny. It’s not impossible, just… harder than it used to be.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I wouldn’t go that far. I’ve laughed here and there, but it’s not the same easy, light feeling I used to have. Most of the time I’m just too worn out or worried to really see the humor in anything.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes—like when my sister said she’d drop off coffee tomorrow, I felt a little spark of “oh, that’ll be nice.” But it’s pretty fleeting. Most plans just feel like more items on a to-do list rather than something I truly look forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t settle for his nap and I kept thinking maybe I’m doing the whole routine wrong, or that he can sense I’m stressed. I know it’s probably not really my fault, but the thought still pops in—like I should be handling everything better.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

It’s not constant, but yes—there are stretches where my heart’s racing and I can’t pin down why. Like last night, baby was breathing fine, sound asleep, and I still got up three times to check. I knew it was irrational, but I couldn’t shake the “what if.”
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—more like a low-grade “on edge” feeling. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my chest feels tight, wondering if the baby’s too quiet or if I missed something. It passes, but it’s unsettling while it’s happening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Some days, yeah. Feeding, changing, trying to sleep in tiny windows—it piles up. I usually manage, but by late afternoon I’ll catch myself thinking, “I can’t do one more round.” I still do it, but it feels heavier than I expected.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s not every night, but a few times this week I’ve lain there wired, running through everything I might have messed up, and it takes forever to drift off. Once I’m asleep I’m okay, but getting there feels hard.
I have felt sad or miserable
I get waves of it—mostly in the evenings when the house is quiet and I’m finally sitting down. It’s not all day, but when it hits I feel heavy, like I’m missing the old version of me.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying
Not really. Maybe once this week—when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt completely useless—but it was just a quick tear-up, not a real cry.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, never. I feel overwhelmed sometimes, but I’ve never thought about hurting myself.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 18: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: ___  

Presenting symptoms endorsed:  
- Persistent low mood with evening “waves” of sadness and sense of “missing old self”  
- Marked reduction in ability to laugh/feel enjoyment; pleasure described as “fleeting”  
- Excessive self-blame regarding infant care; guilt over perceived inadequacy  
- Recurrent, unprovoked anxiety with physical tension, heart-racing, nocturnal safety-checking, “on-edge” sensation  
- Mild sleep-onset difficulty linked to ruminating thoughts of failure  
- Intermittent tearfulness (no full crying spells)  
- Denies thoughts of self-harm or harm to infant  

Pattern: Symptoms cluster consistent with mild-to-moderate postpartum depression with prominent anxiety features; functioning maintained but effortful.  

Risk factors identified: Low mood, anhedonia, guilt, anxiety/panic equivalents, sleep disruption, sense of being overwhelmed.  

Safety: No self-harm ideation reported. Continue monitoring for escalation of mood or anxiety symptoms and emergence of suicidal/harm thoughts.
